title: Crew Output Set by the Least Efficient
statement:
There are n engineers. Engineer i has a speed speed[i] and an efficiency efficiency[i].

You may form a crew of at least 1 and at most k engineers. A crew's output is the sum of its speeds multiplied by the smallest efficiency among its members.

Return the largest output any crew can reach. The limits are chosen so the answer fits in a normal number, so no modulo is needed.

examples.why: Engineers with speeds 2 and 6: (2 + 6) × min(7, 5) = 40. Taking the fastest engineer (speed 9) drags the efficiency down to 1.
Two engineers give (5 + 5) × 4 = 40. Adding the third would give 15 × 2 = 30, so using fewer than k is better.

hints: Fix who has the smallest efficiency in the crew. What should the rest of the crew look like?
If engineer e is the weakest link, everyone else must have efficiency at least e's. Among those, you want the fastest k − 1.
Sort by efficiency from high to low. Walk down the list, keeping the k fastest speeds seen so far in a min-heap with a running sum. Each engineer you reach is the current minimum efficiency.

explain.intuition:
The product has two parts pulling against each other. The trick is to fix one of them. Say engineer e has the lowest efficiency in the crew. Then everyone else must be at least as efficient as e, and among them you simply want the largest speeds, up to k people in total.

Sort engineers by efficiency, highest first. As you walk down, each new engineer is less efficient than everyone already passed, so it is the candidate minimum. Keep the k largest speeds seen so far in a min-heap with their sum: when the heap overflows, drop its slowest. Then sum × current efficiency is the best crew whose weakest link is the current engineer (or better, which only helps).
steps: Pair each speed with its efficiency and sort by efficiency, highest first.
Walk the sorted list. Push the speed into a min-heap and add it to sum.
If the heap holds more than k speeds, pop the smallest and subtract it.
Update the answer with sum × efficiency of the current engineer.
pitfalls: Forcing exactly k members. The second example shows a smaller crew can win.
Worrying that the pop may remove the current engineer. It is harmless: that sum then only holds more efficient engineers, a crew already scored earlier with a higher multiplier.
Sorting speeds alone and taking the top k: speed and efficiency must stay paired.

solutions.title: Try every weakest link, rescan
solutions.idea: For each engineer as the minimum efficiency, collect the speeds of everyone at least as efficient, sort them and take the top k.

solutions.title: Sort by efficiency, heap of top speeds
solutions.idea: Walk engineers from most to least efficient. A min-heap keeps the k largest speeds seen so far and their sum; the current engineer's efficiency is the crew minimum.

followups: The original version allows speeds up to 100 000 and asks for the answer modulo 1 000 000 007. Why must you take the modulo only at the very end, not while comparing?
What if each crew must have exactly k members?
